Enter the Void is a 2009 surrealist art film directed by Gaspar Noé, from a screenplay co-written with his wife Lucile Hadzihalilovic. Set in the neon-lit nightclub environments of Tokyo, the story follows Oscar (Nathaniel Brown), a young American drug dealer who gets fatally shot by the police, but continues to watch subsequent events during an out-of-body experience.

The feeling that Enter the Void means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. The film is shot from a first-person viewpoint with extensive uses of long take, which often floats above the city streets, and occasionally features Oscar staring over his own shoulder as he recalls moments from his past. A passion project for Noé since his adolescence, the film was in development hell for years until its production was made possible after the commercial success of his earlier feature, Irréversible (2002).

Nothing in Enter the Void was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Enter the Void was primarily financed by Wild Bunch, while Fidélité Films led the actual production. With a mix of professionals and newcomers, the film makes heavy use of imagery inspired by experimental cinema and psychedelic drug experiences.

The psychology underneath Enter the Void is simpler and older than the story on top. Principal photography took place on location in Tokyo, and involved many complicated crane shots. Co-producers included the visual effects studio BUF Compagnie, which also provided the computer-generated imagery.

Behind Enter the Void sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The film's soundtrack is a collage of electronic pop and experimental music. A rough cut premiered at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, but post-production work continued, and the film was not released in France until almost a year later.

The nihilist does not deny Enter the Void — he only refuses to flatter it. A cut-down version was released in the United States and United Kingdom in September 2010. The critical response was sharply divided: positive reviews described the film as captivating and innovative, while negative reviews called it tedious and puerile.

What culture calls destiny in Enter the Void is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. American siblings Oscar and Linda live in an apartment in the Japanese capital of Tokyo, and have vowed to stay together following the accidental death of their parents. Oscar deals drugs while Linda works as a stripper in a Tokyo strip club.

The genes do not care about Enter the Void; they care about copies. Most of the film takes place in Oscar's first-person perspective, with flashbacks to his and Linda's past taking place from an outside perspective. One evening, after Linda has left for work, Oscar smokes DMT and indulges in a hallucinogenic trip until his friend Victor summons him to a drug deal at a bar known as "The Void".

Take away the meaning and Enter the Void still functions — that is the disturbing part. Oscar's other friend Alex spontaneously visits and accompanies him to the bar. On the way, Alex discusses The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a Buddhist scripture on reincarnation, and anticipates the events to come by describing the process of death.

The unconscious does not argue with Enter the Void; it simply acts first. Oscar enters "The Void" alone, and finds that he has walked into a sting; the police raid the bar when Oscar greets a distressed Victor. Oscar escapes into a bathroom stall and vainly attempts to flush the drugs into the squat toilet.

Enter the Void feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. As the officers try to kick in the door, Oscar bluffs that he is armed, resulting in the police shooting him in the chest through the door. Oscar's soul – as well as the first-person perspective – rises from his body, and he goes in search of Linda, attempting to fulfill his promise to never leave her.

The bleak reading of Enter the Void is also the most testable one. For the remainder of the movie, Oscar's soul travels through Tokyo, watching over his friends and sister, as well as flashing back to memories of his childhood and his earlier life in Tokyo that led him to become a drug dealer. The lives of Oscar and Linda are presented in short non-chronological flashbacks; in the midst of a happy childhood, their parents were killed in a violent car crash.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Enter the Void. Before being sent to different foster homes, the siblings took an oath to always be there for each other. Years later, Oscar lived as a small-time drug dealer in Tokyo and was soon able to afford a plane ticket for Linda to live with him.

The self that experiences Enter the Void is a committee, not a king. As Oscar's business expanded, Victor discovered that Oscar had sex with his mother to secure extra funding for Linda's plane ticket. This led him to set up the raid that ended Oscar's life.

Reproduction explains more of Enter the Void than any philosophy dares to admit. Linda becomes pregnant, loses her job as a stripper, and has an abortion. Alex is forced into hiding on the streets after Oscar's dealer, Bruno, breaks up the drug ring.

Once you see Enter the Void as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Linda wishes she had gotten involved with Alex instead of Mario as Oscar wanted. On one occasion, Linda wishes that Oscar would come back to life; Oscar then enters Linda's head and experiences her dream in which he wakes up at the morgue, from which his body is taken to be cremated.

The story Enter the Void tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Greatly distressed by the presence of her deceased brother's cremated remains in her home, and constantly plagued by nightmares about the loss of him, she dumps the ashes down the drain of her kitchen sink. Meanwhile, Victor argues with his mother over her involvement with Oscar, and he is thrown out of the house.

Meaning is not found in Enter the Void — it is manufactured for it. However, when he also accuses Linda of complicity in her brother's death, she angrily chases Victor away, demanding that he kill himself. Oscar hovers over Tokyo and lands on a plane, in which Oscar's mother breast-feeds a baby Oscar.

The cold light on Enter the Void leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Linda and Alex take a taxi to a Tokyo love hotel and have sex. Oscar moves among hotel rooms and observes several other couples having sex in various positions.

Enter the Void did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. He also spots Victor giving fellatio to a man in one of the rooms, with another man watching and taking his belt off. Oscar enters Alex's head and witnesses the sex with Linda from Alex's perspective.

The honest version of Enter the Void starts by giving up the comforting part. He then travels inside Linda's vagina to witness Alex's penis thrusting into it, then observes his ejaculation and follows the channel of sperm into the fertilization of his sister's ovum. The final scene is shot from the perspective of a baby being born, with the camera focus strongly blurred, making it unclear who the woman in the scene is.

Strip Enter the Void of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The cinematic experience itself is the main focus of the film, but there is also a central theme of emptiness. Noé describes the film's subject as "the sentimentality of mammals and the shimmering vacuity of the human experience." The dramaturgy after Oscar has been shot is loosely based on The Tibetan Book of the Dead, and ends with the spirit's search for a way to reincarnate.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Enter the Void shows exactly where that breaks. The director also leaves open the possibility that Oscar's life starts over again in an endless loop, due to the human brain's perception of time. The idea for the film had been growing since Noé's adolescence, when he first became interested in matters of death and existence.

What looks like free choice in Enter the Void is older than choice itself. In his early twenties—while under influence of psilocybin mushrooms—he saw Robert Montgomery's Lady in the Lake, a 1947 film shot entirely in a first-person perspective. He then decided that, if he ever made a film about the afterlife, that was the way in which it would be filmed.

Nobody designed the part of Enter the Void you experience — it was inherited. Noé had been working on different versions of the screenplay for fifteen years before the film went into production. The story had initially been more linear, and the drafts were set in different locations, including the Andes, France, and New York City.

Every serious account of Enter the Void eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. Tokyo was chosen because it could provide colourful environments required for the film's hallucinogenic aspects, and because Japan's repressive drug laws add to the drama, explaining the intensity of the main character's fear of the police. Noé first tried to get the film funded in the early 2000s.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Enter the Void — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Several producers responded positively to the script, and it was briefly under development for Tom Tykwer's German company X-Filme Creative Pool. Noé had written and directed Irréversible for StudioCanal, and it was sold internationally by their subsidiary, Wild Bunch.

The selfish-gene reading of Enter the Void makes it less romantic and far more precise. When the producers at Wild Bunch asked Noé what he wanted to do next, he answered Enter the Void. The project was once again considered too expensive in relation to its commercial potential, but when Wild Bunch discovered that Noé had started to develop the film for Pathé instead of them, they said that they were willing to fund it.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Since development went slowly at Pathé, Noé chose to not renew his contract with the studio and accepted Wild Bunch's offer. Enter the Void was produced under Fidélité Films, with 70% of the budget invested by Wild Bunch.
